Q051.L1t: Parking enforcement worldwide uses a range of tools, including fines, towing and physical restraints, to deter illegal parking.
Q051.L2t: Wheel-immobilizing devices for vehicles were first used in the United States in the 1950s as a way to deal with unpaid parking tickets.
Q051.L3t: The device police use is a large metal clamp that locks onto a wheel so the car cannot be driven, and it is named after the Colorado city where it first came into use.
Q051.L4t: The metal wheel-immobilizing device police use on repeat parking offenders is the Denver boot.
Q051.L2f: Wheel-immobilizing devices were first introduced in Europe in the 1990s and were originally made of hardened rubber rather than metal.
Q051.L3f: The device police use on repeat offenders is a tracking unit hidden in the vehicle that lets officers find and recover the car, rather than a clamp fitted to a wheel.
Q051.L4f: The device police use to immobilize the wheels of repeat parking offenders is LoJack.

Q052.L1t: Geometry classifies angles by their size, measured in degrees, and each kind has its own name.
Q052.L2t: Perpendicular lines are lines in the same plane that intersect each other at a single point.
Q052.L3t: Perpendicular lines meet so that each of the four angles they form measures exactly 90 degrees, which is a quarter of a full turn.
Q052.L4t: Two perpendicular lines form a right angle where they meet.
Q052.L2f: Perpendicular lines can never cross each other, because lines that intersect are always parallel in the same plane.
Q052.L3f: Perpendicular lines meet at an angle of less than 90 degrees, so the angle they form is smaller than a quarter turn.
Q052.L4f: Two perpendicular lines form an acute angle where they meet.

Q053.L1t: Fast food companies in the United States have long competed through memorable television advertising campaigns and catchphrases.
Q053.L2t: The 'Where's the beef?' slogan appeared in a television commercial in 1984 and became a popular catchphrase, even being used in that year's presidential campaign.
Q053.L3t: The ad showed an elderly woman looking at a burger with a huge bun and a tiny patty, and it was made for a chain whose founder, Dave Thomas, named it after his daughter.
Q053.L4t: Wendy's was the fast food chain that used the slogan 'Where's the beef?'
Q053.L2f: The 'Where's the beef?' commercial first aired in the 1960s and starred a cartoon mascot instead of real people.
Q053.L3f: The 'Where's the beef?' ad was made for a chain founded by Colonel Harland Sanders, whose fried chicken is sold in buckets and whose face is on the logo.
Q053.L4f: Kentucky Fried Chicken was the fast food chain that used the slogan 'Where's the beef?'
